svg.title: One word: queue or stack
svg.desc: A whiteboard sketch showing the same seven-node graph twice, once visited in breadth-first level order with dashed level rings and the word QUEUE circled, once visited in depth-first order with the word STACK circled, and the two nearly identical code fragments differing only in popleft versus pop; a topological sort peeling zero-in-degree nodes off a five-node directed graph with in-degrees written under each; the same graph with one red back edge added leaving three nodes whose in-degree never reaches zero, ringed in red as the cycle; and a memory comparison of 52.3 megabytes for an adjacency list against 1,250 megabytes for a bitset adjacency matrix.
svg.text: visits by LEVEL -> the first time you reach a node
goes DEEP down one branch first ->
finds A path, not the shortest one
remove every in-degree 0, decrement its neighbours, repeat
the order you removed them in IS the answer: A B C D E
add ONE back edge and the same algorithm finds the
3 nodes never reach in-degree 0. THAT is the
23.9x - and the matrix only wins if the graph is DENSE
BFS over 2M directed edges: 159.4 ms = 80 ns per edge
BFS and DFS are the same three lines - that one word is the whole difference.
...week 30: a cycle in your agent's step graph = tokens burning forever
